metadata.title: The Judgment Is the Job.

metadata.color_semantics: Fidelity claude palette. ONE terracotta #D97757 event per beat, and it always marks JUDGMENT — the part that did not move to the machine. The accent carries the thesis rather than decorating the frame.
metadata.note: ILLUSTRATE LAW: Claude UI appears at B00 (cold open, with RESULT lines), B03 (ask micro-beat of the one ask->result pair), B07 (verdict), B08 (handoff), B09 (outro). Every other beat illustrates. HONESTY (user constraint, 2026-08-20): NO statistics, percentages, or counts anywhere — every comparison is ordinal or described in words ('dramatically faster', 'increasingly obsolete'). See FACTCHECK.md.

beats.narration_text: A tagline used to take a week and a room full of people. Now it takes a sentence. So are copywriters and art directors finished? Today — what AI took, and what it couldn't.

show.event: Cream page, spark, serif greeting 'Namaste, Yatra' settles above the composer
The ask types itself in, character by character
Terracotta send button arms — the ONE accent event
Running indicator: 'separating execution from judgment…'
Three result lines stagger in — the ask lands ANSWERED (COLD OPEN LAW)

props.command: I run creative for a mid-size brand. AI now drafts our ad copy, taglines and social posts, and generates visual concepts too. Be blunt: which parts of my copywriters' and designers' jobs has this actually replaced, which parts has it left untouched, and what should I stop paying people to do?
output: replaced: producing options — copy, variants, concepts
untouched: deciding which one is right, and owning it
the job moved from making to judging

beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Yatra, and this video is about what AI actually did to advertising — and what it means for your job. The short version: AI didn't replace copywriting or art direction, it replaced the execution. The judgment is still yours. Stay with me and you'll know which half of your work just got cheap, and which half to sell instead.

show.event: Serif frame holds while the narrator introduces herself by name and states what the video is about and what the viewer will get from it
On the spoken word 'execution', the node SPLITS into two tracks that visibly diverge
Upper track 'EXECUTION — drafting, variants, concepting' dives toward the floor in ink
Lower track 'JUDGMENT — is it true, is it us, will you sign it' climbs in terracotta — the ONE accent
The gap between the tracks holds ≥2s — the whole reel lives in that gap

data.slideMeta: THE SPLIT · one job became two
data.script: The job moved. It didn't vanish.

beats.narration_text: So split the work in two. On one side, producing options — headlines, taglines, a month of social variants, translations. AI is dramatically faster at all of it. On the other side, choosing: which claim survives legal, which voice sounds like us, which idea is actually good. That side hasn't moved.

show.event: A vertical rule draws down the centre; two column headings type in
Left column fills in ink, item by item, as each is named: headlines, taglines, social variants, translations
Right column fills in terracotta as each is named: survives legal, sounds like us, actually good
Footer line lands: 'the left column got faster · the right column did not move'. Held ≥2s

data.slideMeta: The two halves of the work
data.title: Producing options · Choosing one
data.note: the left column got dramatically faster · the right column did not move

beats.narration_text: So I asked Claude for ad creative — not one concept, but every concept it could give me for the same brief.

show.event: Composer framed; spark line reads 'Every concept.'
The generation prompt types itself in — the ACTUAL prompt behind the next beat
Terracotta send arms; runningText 'concepting…' — cut to RESULT

props.command: Brief: launch a reusable water bottle for city commuters. Give me a wall of distinct visual ad concepts — different angles, different emotional registers — as concept cards I can react to. Don't pick a favourite. That part is my job.

beats.narration_text: This is the shift in one picture. A wall of concepts, faster than a designer could sketch one. None of them is finished, and the machine has no opinion about which is right. Getting options on the wall used to be the expensive part. The wall is free now. Choosing is not.

show.event: Concept cards pop onto a grid in rapid succession, each with a different angle label — the wall fills faster than the voice can list it
All cards sit equal and unranked; nothing is highlighted — the machine has no opinion
On the spoken word 'choosing', ONE card takes a terracotta ring — the human's pick, the ONE accent
Caption lands beneath: 'the wall is free · choosing is not'. Held ≥2s

data.slideMeta: One brief · a wall of concepts
data.title: The wall is free
data.caption: the wall is free · choosing is not

beats.narration_text: So what happens to the copywriter and the designer? Two futures. If the job is described as producing assets, that description is increasingly obsolete — and so is the rate card. If it's described as owning the brief and the final call, it just gained leverage. Same person. Different job description.

show.event: Question card lands: 'How is the job described?'
Branch one draws down-left: 'I produce the assets' — the B02 left column ghosts in behind it
Branch two draws down-right: 'I own the standard and the call' — the B02 right column ghosts in behind it, in terracotta
Resolver types in beneath: 'the description is the whole difference'. Both branches held side-by-side ≥2s

branches.label: I produce the assets
branches.fix: Increasingly obsolete — so is the rate card.

branches.label: I own the standard
branches.detail: Paid for the brief and the final call.
branches.fix: More leverage than before, not less.

resolver.label: The description is the whole difference
resolver.detail: Same skills. What changed is which half of the work you're selling.

beats.narration_text: And here's where it breaks. Four things the machine cannot own. Whether a claim is actually true. Whether it sounds like you across a year, not one post. Whether it lands in a culture it doesn't live in. And who answers when it's wrong. If your work has none of those, you're exposed.

show.event: Four numbered rows draw in one at a time, each landing ON its spoken phrase, terracotta marker at the left of each
Each row's one-line 'why' types in beneath its heading
The self-test lands last and holds: 'none of these in your work → exposed · mostly these → fine'. Held ≥2s

data.slideMeta: Where this breaks · what the machine cannot own
data.title: Four things it cannot own

items.label: Whether the claim is true
items.why: The model will phrase a false claim beautifully.

items.label: Whether it sounds like you
items.why: Consistency across a year, not one post.

items.label: Whether it lands
items.why: It does not live in the culture it is writing to.

items.label: Who answers when it's wrong
items.why: Accountability cannot be delegated to a tool.

data.closer: None of these in your work → exposed.  Mostly these → fine.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap. One — AI replaced the execution of copy and creative, not the judgment about it. Two — producing options is cheap now; choosing among them is the whole job. Three — a role defined as making assets is shrinking; one defined as owning the standard is growing. This is a shift described, not predicted.

show.event: Claude artifact page opens on the cream ground
Four verdict lines stagger in, one per spoken clause
The caveat line lands last and holds

props.artifactTitle: The Judgment Is the Job. — one page
artifactLines: Execution — drafting, variants, concepting — moved to the machine, and is dramatically faster there.
Judgment — is it true, is it us, will you sign it — did not move at all.
A role defined as making assets is shrinking. A role defined as owning the standard is growing.
Caveat: a shift in progress, described — not a prediction with a date, and no numbers are claimed here.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this: take my last five pieces of ad copy or creative, and for each one tell me which part was execution AI could now produce, and which part was judgment only a person could make. Then grade it: does it split every piece, does it disagree with you anywhere, and would a client pay for the leftover?

show.event: Serif 'Your turn.' replaces the persona greeting — viewer-addressed
The prompt types itself in as the narration reads it aloud, verbatim
Terracotta send arms; runningText 'paste this into Claude…'
Three-item rubric stacks in beneath the composer as each check is spoken
